newsitem.title: UK: Tributes pour in for cameraman "Mo" Amin.
newsitem.headline: Tributes pour in for cameraman "Mo" Amin.

text.p: Mohamed Amin, a Kenyan television cameraman who died aboard a hijacked plane that crashed in the Indian Ocean, was one of the best front-line photographers in the business, journalists who worked with him said on Sunday.
"Mo" Amin's dramatic television pictures of starving and dying Ethiopians in 1984 helped alert the world to the famine there.

Amin, 53, was on an Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 seized by three hijackers on a flight from Addis Ababa to Nairobi on Saturday. The airliner ran out of fuel and went down in the sea just off the Comoro Islands.
Only 52 out of 175 passengers and crew on board were reported to have survived.
Michael Buerk, a reporter and newsreader for BBC television who worked with Amin on many assignements, said:
"It is ironic that somebody who survived so many dangerous assignments should have been killed by a news story he hadn't gone to cover -- a million-to-one chance, a botched hijacking."
In a televised BBC tribute to Amin, Buerk said: "I was with him when he lost several of his nine lives. He was one of the greatest of front-line cameramen.
"He was brilliant, he was brave, he was human and very, very driven."
Tony Hall, chief executive of BBC News, said: "No news cameraman in recent years has had a greater impact than Mohamed Amin. His pictures from Ethiopia 12 years ago moved the world."
Hall added: "He was a warm, witty and generous man. He will be a great loss to the industry and his many friends and colleagues, as well as his family."
Amin's Ethiopian pictures jolted the world into a huge relief effort that included the "Live Aid" rock concert broadcast around the world.
Organiser Bob Geldof remembered how Amin's pictures had moved him. "Mo Amin succeeded above all else in showing his own disgust and shame and anger and making it yours also," he said.
"Many millions are alive today because Mo Amin risked his life time and again," said former U.S. president George Bush, who was vice-president in 1984.
Amin, a self-taught photographer, worked for Reuters after it took over the television film agency Visnews, later renamed Reuters Television, in 1993.
Reuters Editor-in-Chief Mark Wood said: "We are deeply saddened by his death.
"Mohamed Amin was one of the outstanding newsmen of his time. He was known everywhere, hugely respected, an extraordinary and forceful person.
"He transformed television coverage of Africa and, by focusing the world's attention on famine and suffering, helped to save many lives."
